04 · Cohorts and observed lifetime value¶

How customers who started in different months and channels keep buying and build up value, which cohorts are genuinely new customers, and what that means for the New Customers second-order journey and the coupon test in the autumn plan.

Cohorts 2018-10 to 2020-08, activity to 2020-08 · money in CU (price × 590), gross demand · reads the built marts in data/marts/

TL;DR¶

  • The early cohorts are mostly existing customers, not newcomers. The data starts on 2018-09-20, so the 2018-10 "cohort" has 212K customers against 23-52K a month from 2019-03 onwards, and it is still 30% active in month 12 against 12-15% for 2019 cohorts. Anything said about newcomers uses cohorts from 2019-03 onwards.
  • Online-first customers build more observed value: 209 CU in 12 months against 165 CU for store-first (cohorts 2019-01 to 2019-08, gross demand). 29 CU of the 45 CU gap is already there in the first month, so it is mostly the bigger first basket rather than a different repeat pattern.
  • The second order is the biggest hurdle. Of 292K likely new customers (first order March-September 2019), 38% never placed a second order within a year; of those who placed two, 69% went on to a third.
  • The spring 2020 closure moved acquisition online. The 2020-04 cohort (40.7K, the largest since 2019-07) was 100% online-first and 2020-03 86%. Their month-1 retention (14-16% for online-first) is in the range of the late-2019 online cohorts (11-15%), so nothing yet marks them as weaker customers.
  • For the New Customers journey and the coupon test: 40% of likely new customers place a second order within 90 days of the first, 11% within six days, before the journey starts on day 7. Customers who came back by day 90 spent 129 CU in days 91-365 against 46 CU for those who did not. That gap is self-selection, not the effect of a coupon, which is why the coupon cell is judged on 12-month value as well as on the 90-day second-order rate.

Question¶

Do customers who started in different months, or in different channels, keep buying at different rates and build up different value? And what does that mean for the New Customers part of the autumn plan: a welcome journey whose only goal is the second order, plus a test cell with 10% off the second order?

This is the supplement to the CRM Manager's request ("give me segments, a recommendation per segment, and how we will measure the campaign"): it checks the evidence behind the plan's view that the second order is where a discount is most likely to pay, which is why one of the two coupon test cells sits there.

Data¶

  • Source: H&M Personalized Fashion Recommendations dataset (Kaggle, 2022): transactions from 2018-09-20 to 2020-09-22.
  • cohort_retention mart (sql/11_cohort_retention.sql): one row per first-order month × first-order channel × month number. 23 cohorts from 2018-10 to 2020-08 (the 11-day 2018-09 cohort and the partial 2020-09 are dropped); activity is counted up to 2020-08. Review List accounts (bulk or near-daily buying, kept in all other totals) are left out of the cohorts.
  • order_ladder mart (src/rfm/analysis.py): the chance of one more order within 12 months of the first, for two cohorts with a full year of follow-up.
  • fct_orders and dim_customers for the time-to-second-order look-up, and campaign_economics for the New Customers arms.
  • Definitions: money in CU = price × 590, gross demand (the data has no returns). An order is one customer, one day, one channel. First-order channel = Online, Store, or Both (both channels on the first day). Store purchases are only visible when the shopper identifies as a member.

from rfm.sqlrun import query, run_sql_file

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", message="The kopts argument is ignored")  # kaleido notice on every PNG export

M = D.metrics()
coh = D.mart("cohort_retention")
coh["cohort"] = pd.to_datetime(coh["cohort_month"]).dt.strftime("%Y-%m")
coh["calendar_month"] = (pd.PeriodIndex(pd.to_datetime(coh["cohort_month"]), freq="M") + coh["month_number"].to_numpy()).astype(str)


def sql_section(path: str, start: str, end: str, ahead: int = 0) -> None:
    """Print a SQL file from the first line containing `start` to the next line containing `end` (plus `ahead` lines)."""
    lines = (ROOT / path).read_text().splitlines()
    i = next(k for k, line in enumerate(lines) if start in line)
    j = next(k for k in range(i, len(lines)) if end in lines[k]) + ahead
    print(f"-- {path}, lines {i + 1}-{j + 1}")
    print("\n".join(lines[i:j + 1]))


def table(df: pd.DataFrame, formats: dict | None = None):
    """Display a frame without its index, with per-column formats; missing values as '-'."""
    return df.style.format(formats or {}, na_rep="-").hide(axis="index")


def retention(frame: pd.DataFrame, months=(1, 2, 3, 6, 12)) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Share of each cohort active in month M (all first-order channels in `frame` pooled)."""
    size = frame[frame.month_number == 0].groupby("cohort")["cohort_customers"].sum()
    act = frame.groupby(["cohort", "month_number"])["active_customers"].sum().unstack()
    return act.div(size, axis=0).reindex(columns=list(months)).add_prefix("M")


print(f"{coh.cohort.nunique()} cohorts, {coh.cohort.min()} to {coh.cohort.max()}; "
      f"{coh.loc[coh.month_number == 0, 'cohort_customers'].sum():,} customers; activity to {coh.calendar_month.max()}")

23 cohorts, 2018-10 to 2020-08; 1,203,792 customers; activity to 2020-08

Method¶

  1. Cohort = the month of a customer's first order seen in the data.
  2. Retention in month M = share of the cohort with at least one order in the M-th calendar month after the cohort month (M1 = the next calendar month). It is not cumulative: a customer can be inactive in M2 and active again in M3.
  3. Observed lifetime value (LTV) = cumulative revenue per cohort customer, month by month, gross demand. It is what customers actually spent, not a forecast, and it only covers months that every cohort in the range has completed.
  4. Order ladder = of the customers with n orders within 12 months of their first order, the share who place order n+1 in that same window.
  5. Likely new customers = first order from 2019-03-01 to 2019-09-22, i.e. no order in the 5+ months of data before; this is the cleanest newcomer group the data allows, not a guarantee.
  6. Time to second order = days from the first to the second order for the likely-new group, within 12 months.

The cohort definition and the order ladder as they run in the pipeline:

In [2]:
sql_section("sql/11_cohort_retention.sql", "customers AS (", "JOIN monthly m USING (customer_id)", ahead=2)

-- sql/11_cohort_retention.sql, lines 27-62
    customers AS (
        SELECT
            customer_id,
            DATE_TRUNC('month', first_order_date)::DATE AS cohort_month,
            first_order_channel
        FROM 'data/marts/dim_customers.parquet'
        WHERE has_orders
          AND NOT is_excluded
          AND first_order_date >= DATE '2018-10-01'
          AND first_order_date <  DATE '2020-09-01'
    ),
    monthly AS (
        SELECT
            customer_id,
            DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date)::DATE AS activity_month,
            SUM(revenue_cents)                    AS revenue_cents
        FROM 'data/marts/fct_orders.parquet'
        WHERE order_date < DATE '2020-09-01'
        GROUP BY ALL
    ),
    cohort_size AS (
        SELECT cohort_month, first_order_channel, COUNT(*) AS cohort_customers
        FROM customers
        GROUP BY ALL
    ),
    activity AS (
        SELECT
            c.cohort_month,
            c.first_order_channel,
            DATE_DIFF('month', c.cohort_month, m.activity_month) AS month_number,
            COUNT(DISTINCT m.customer_id)                        AS active_customers,
            SUM(m.revenue_cents)                                 AS revenue_cents
        FROM customers c
        JOIN monthly m USING (customer_id)
        GROUP BY ALL
    )
In [3]:
print(inspect.getsource(analysis.order_ladder))

def order_ladder() -> pd.DataFrame:
    """P(at least n+1 orders | at least n orders) within 12 months of the first order.

    Two cohorts, both with a full 12-month follow-up:
      'first order 2018-09-20 to 2019-09-22'  everyone whose first order *in the data* is in year 1
                                              (includes existing customers: left-censoring)
      'new: first order 2019-03-01 to 2019-09-22' no order in the 5+ months before, so mostly
                                              genuinely new customers
    """
    return query("""
        WITH first AS (
            SELECT customer_id, first_order_date,
                   CASE WHEN first_order_date >= DATE '2019-03-01'
                        THEN 'new: first order 2019-03-01 to 2019-09-22' END AS clean_cohort
            FROM 'data/marts/dim_customers.parquet'
            WHERE has_orders AND NOT is_excluded AND first_order_date <= DATE '2019-09-22'
        ),
        n_orders AS (
            SELECT f.customer_id, f.clean_cohort, COUNT(*) AS orders_12m_after_first
            FROM first f
            JOIN 'data/marts/fct_orders.parquet' o
              ON o.customer_id = f.customer_id
             AND o.order_date >= f.first_order_date
             AND o.order_date <  f.first_order_date + 365
            GROUP BY 1, 2
        ),
        tagged AS (
            SELECT 'first order 2018-09-20 to 2019-09-22' AS cohort, orders_12m_after_first FROM n_orders
            UNION ALL
            SELECT clean_cohort, orders_12m_after_first FROM n_orders WHERE clean_cohort IS NOT NULL
        ),
        ladder AS (
            SELECT c.cohort, k AS orders,
                   (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM tagged t WHERE t.cohort = c.cohort AND t.orders_12m_after_first >= k) AS customers
            FROM (SELECT DISTINCT cohort FROM tagged) c, range(1, 11) r(k)
        )
        SELECT cohort, orders, customers,
               LEAD(customers) OVER (PARTITION BY cohort ORDER BY orders) / customers AS p_next_order
        FROM ladder ORDER BY cohort, orders
    """)

Results¶

1. Cohort sizes, and why the early cohorts are not new customers¶

The data has no "customer since" date, so a customer's first order in the data is used. For a customer who has shopped for years, that is simply their first purchase after 2018-09-20. If the early cohorts were newcomers, their size would be similar to later ones.

Takeaway: The first three cohorts hold 440K customers against 23-52K a month from 2019-03 onwards, and the 2018-10 cohort is still 30% active in month 12 against 12-15% for the 2019 cohorts: the early rows are mostly existing customers seen for the first time, so newcomer retention is read from 2019-03 onwards.

2. Retention in the first year¶

Each cell is the share of a cohort that bought in that later month; read across a row to see one cohort fade, down a column to compare cohorts at the same age.

In [5]:
C.cohort_heatmap(coh, 12)

Takeaway: Month-1 retention ranges from 12% to 36%, but from 2019-03 onwards newcomers start at 12-21% in month 1 and fade to 10-15% by month 6; the darker 2018 rows are a different population, not better acquisition.

3. The full window, and the calendar effect¶

Over 22 months the diagonals are calendar months: every cohort lives through the same seasons and the same store closure.

In [6]:
C.cohort_heatmap(coh, 22)

Takeaway: The long view keeps the 2018-10 cohort at 22-36% a month while newcomer cohorts settle around 10-15%, and calendar months run diagonally through every row (the June 2020 reopening is darker in every cohort, e.g. 2019-06: 12% in May, 15% in June), so a cohort's later months mix its age with what happened in that calendar month.

The closure shows most clearly when newcomers are split by the channel of their first order (cohorts 2019-03 to 2019-12 pooled, share active in each calendar month of 2020):

In [7]:

4. Observed lifetime value by first channel¶

Cumulative revenue per customer for the 2019-01 to 2019-08 cohorts, the latest ones with 12 full months of follow-up.

In [8]:
C.ltv_curves(coh, "2019-01-01", "2019-08-01", 12)

Takeaway: Online-first customers reach 209 CU in 12 months against 165 CU for store-first, and 29 CU of that 45 CU gap is already there in the first month, so it is mostly the bigger first basket; the 322 CU for customers who used both channels on their first day is real but covers only 1,861 customers (0.5% of these cohorts).

In [9]:
def ltv(frame: pd.DataFrame, first: str, last: str, months: int) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Cumulative revenue per cohort customer by first-order channel (same arithmetic as C.ltv_curves)."""
    d = frame[frame.cohort.between(first, last)]
    n = d[d.month_number == 0].groupby("first_order_channel")["cohort_customers"].sum()
    rev = d[d.month_number <= months].pivot_table(index="month_number", columns="first_order_channel", values="revenue_cu", aggfunc="sum")
    out = rev.cumsum().div(n)[["Online", "Store", "Both"]]
    out["Gap online - store"] = out["Online"] - out["Store"]
    return out

The same pattern as in the segment view (notebook 03, section 5): an online order is about twice a store basket, so online-first customers start higher; after month 0 the gap only widens from 29 to 45 CU (online-first customers add 130 CU over the next 12 months, store-first 114 CU). First channel describes customers; it is not a lever, and nothing here shows that moving a customer's first purchase online would add value.

5. A later range: cohorts 2019-09 to 2020-02¶

Cleaner newcomer cohorts (about a year or more without an order before joining), with six months of follow-up that run through the closure.

In [10]:
C.ltv_curves(coh, "2019-09-01", "2020-02-01", 6)

Takeaway: The later cohorts keep the same order at a lower level (116 CU online-first vs 93 CU store-first after six months, against 150 vs 114 CU for the 2019-01 to 2019-08 cohorts at the same age), as expected from cohorts that contain fewer existing customers and lived through a closure in their first months.

6. The order ladder: likely new customers vs everyone first seen in year 1¶

Of the customers with n orders, how many place one more within 12 months of their first order. Blue = likely new customers (first order March-September 2019); grey = everyone first seen between 2018-09-20 and 2019-09-22, existing customers included.

In [12]:
lad = D.mart("order_ladder")
C.order_ladder(lad)

Takeaway: For likely new customers the chance of one more order rises from 62% after the first order to 69% after the second and 72% after the third, so the first repeat purchase is the biggest hurdle; everyone first seen in year 1, existing customers included, looks more loyal at every step (72%, 80%, 83%), which is the left-censoring effect again.

7. The 2020 closure cohorts¶

Stores were closed from 2020-03-20 to 2020-05-05. Who joined in those months, and how did they behave in their first months?

Takeaway: With stores shut, the 2020-04 cohort (40.7K, the largest since 2019-07) was 100% online-first and 2020-03 86%. Their online-first month-1 retention (14-16%) sits within or slightly above the late-2019 online cohorts (11-15%), so lockdown sign-ups do not look like a weaker kind of customer, with two caveats: their first months fell in a very different calendar (the reopening and the summer), and they are only four to five months old.

Today's New Customers segment (first order 2020-06-25 to 2020-09-22: 71,117 customers, 66% online only, 33% reachable by email) comes from the summer cohorts after reopening.

8. What this means for the New Customers journey and the coupon test¶

When do newcomers come back? Days from the first to the second order, likely new customers (first order 2019-03-01 to 2019-09-22):

In [15]:
per = query("""
    WITH first AS (
        SELECT customer_id, first_order_date
        FROM 'data/marts/dim_customers.parquet'
        WHERE has_orders AND NOT is_excluded
          AND first_order_date BETWEEN DATE '2019-03-01' AND DATE '2019-09-22'
    ),
    orders AS (
        SELECT f.customer_id, o.order_date - f.first_order_date AS day, o.revenue_cents,
               ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY f.customer_id ORDER BY o.order_date, o.sales_channel_id) AS n
        FROM first f
        JOIN 'data/marts/fct_orders.parquet' o
          ON o.customer_id = f.customer_id
         AND o.order_date >= f.first_order_date
         AND o.order_date <  f.first_order_date + 365
    )
    SELECT customer_id,
           MIN(day) FILTER (WHERE n = 2)                                   AS days_to_second,
           SUM(revenue_cents) / 100.0                                      AS revenue_12m_cu,
           COALESCE(SUM(revenue_cents) FILTER (WHERE day > 90), 0) / 100.0 AS revenue_day_91_365_cu
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY customer_id
""")
assert len(per) == lad.loc[lad.cohort.str.startswith("new") & (lad.orders == 1), "customers"].iloc[0]  # same cohort as the ladder

days = per["days_to_second"].astype("float")
bands = pd.cut(days, [-1, 0, 6, 30, 60, 90, 180, 364],
               labels=["same day (other channel)", "days 1-6", "days 7-30", "days 31-60", "days 61-90", "days 91-180", "days 181-364"])
timing = bands.value_counts(sort=False).rename("customers").to_frame()
timing.loc["no second order within a year"] = int(days.isna().sum())
timing["% of new customers"] = timing["customers"] / len(per)
timing["cumulative"] = timing["% of new customers"].cumsum()
print(f"{len(per):,} likely new customers; median wait among those who return within a year: {days.median():.0f} days")
table(timing.rename_axis("Second order").reset_index(), {"customers": "{:,.0f}", "% of new customers": "{:.1%}", "cumulative": "{:.1%}"})

292,074 likely new customers; median wait among those who return within a year: 51 days

Takeaway: 40% of likely new customers place a second order within 90 days of their first and 62% within a year (median wait 51 days among those who return); 11% come back within six days on their own, before the journey's first email on day 7, and another 29% by day 90, which is the window the journey and the 30-day coupon act in.

Note the different clock: the plan's baseline for New Customers (28.5% buy again within 90 days) is measured from a snapshot date for customers whose first order was 0-89 days earlier, which is how the autumn test will be read; the 40% here is measured from each customer's first order.

What is a second order worth? 12-month revenue of the same customers, split by whether they came back within 90 days:

In [16]:
per["second_by_day_90"] = days.le(90).fillna(False).astype(bool)   # no second order counts as "no"
value = per.groupby("second_by_day_90").agg(customers=("customer_id", "size"), revenue_12m_cu=("revenue_12m_cu", "mean"),
                                            revenue_day_91_365_cu=("revenue_day_91_365_cu", "mean"))
value.index = value.index.map({True: "Second order by day 90", False: "No second order by day 90"})
table(value.rename_axis("Likely new customers").reset_index().rename(columns={
          "customers": "Customers", "revenue_12m_cu": "Revenue in first 12 months (CU)",
          "revenue_day_91_365_cu": "of which days 91-365 (CU)"}),
      {"Customers": "{:,.0f}", "Revenue in first 12 months (CU)": "{:.0f}", "of which days 91-365 (CU)": "{:.0f}"})
Out[16]:
Likely new customers Customers Revenue in first 12 months (CU) of which days 91-365 (CU)
No second order by day 90 175,492 106 46
Second order by day 90 116,582 289 129

Takeaway: Customers who came back by day 90 spent 129 CU in days 91-365 against 46 CU for those who did not. This is selection (keener customers come back sooner), not what a coupon would add, so the economics keep valuing an incremental buyer at one order; but it is why the coupon cell is also judged on 12-month value, since a 90-day read would miss any lasting effect.

How the autumn test is set up for New Customers (from campaign_economics):

In [17]:
econ = D.mart("campaign_economics")
new = econ[econ.audience == "new"]
table(pd.DataFrame({
    "Arm": new.arm, "Role": new.role, "Customers in arm": new.contacted, "Buy anyway (BAU, 90 days)": new.baseline_rate,
    "Assumed lift (pp)": new.uplift_pp, "Break-even lift (pp)": new.breakeven_uplift_pp, "Detectable lift (pp)": new.mde_rate_pp,
    "Expected net profit (CU)": new.net_profit_cu, "Sized for its decision": np.where(new.role == "Test cell", new.powered_for_decision.map({True: "yes", False: "no"}), "-"),
}), {"Customers in arm": "{:,.0f}", "Buy anyway (BAU, 90 days)": "{:.1%}", "Assumed lift (pp)": "{:.1f}", "Break-even lift (pp)": "{:.2f}",
     "Detectable lift (pp)": "{:.2f}", "Expected net profit (CU)": "{:,.0f}"})
Out[17]:
Arm Role Customers in arm Buy anyway (BAU, 90 days) Assumed lift (pp) Break-even lift (pp) Detectable lift (pp) Expected net profit (CU) Sized for its decision
Welcome journey Rollout 32,003 28.5% 1.5 0.99 1.66 3,371 -
Welcome journey + 10% off 2nd order Test cell 32,003 28.5% 3.0 6.07 1.66 -15,208 yes

Takeaway: The coupon cell (32.0K customers) can detect a 1.66 pp lift against a 6.07 pp break-even, so a "no" is informative; at the assumed +3.0 pp it would lose 15.2K CU in 90 days on one-order value, while the journey alone (break-even 0.99 pp, mostly its paid-social cost) is expected to make 3.4K CU.

Limitations¶

  • Left-censoring. A first order in the data is not a first order ever. Cohorts before 2019-03 are mostly existing customers, and even later cohorts can include customers returning after a long gap that started before 2018-09-20.
  • Calendar months, not exact ages. M1 is the next calendar month, so a customer who joined on the 31st has less time than one who joined on the 1st, and seasons and the 2020 closure run diagonally through every cohort.
  • Observed LTV is gross demand and backward-looking. No returns are deducted (typically higher online), follow-up differs by cohort, and it is not a forecast of future value.
  • First-order channel is what we can see. Store purchases are only recorded when the shopper identifies as a member, so some "online-first" customers may have shopped anonymously in store before.
  • Associations, not effects. First channel and an early second order go with higher value, but neither is shown to cause it; the holdout test is what measures the effect of the journey and the coupon.
  • Small groups. Customers who used both channels on their first day are 0.5% of the cohorts, and the closure cohorts are only a few months old.
  • Review List accounts are left out of the cohorts, and same-day online orders collapse into one order.

Recommendations / next step¶

  • Keep the welcome journey focused on the second order and start it on day 7 as planned: it then reaches newcomers after the 11% who come back in the first week on their own, while 29% still place their second order between day 7 and day 90. Make it always-on if its measured lift clears its break-even (0.99 pp, mostly the paid-social cost for the two thirds not on email).
  • Run 10% off the second order only in the test cell. Roll it out only if the 95% lower bound of its lift over the journey-only cell clears break-even, and report the cell's 12-month value at the next quarterly review: a second order is worth more than one order if coupon-driven returners behave like natural ones, which this data cannot show.
  • Quote newcomer retention from 2019-03 onwards and never the late-2018 rows, which are mostly existing customers.
  • Treat lockdown online sign-ups as ordinary online newcomers and re-check the 2020-03 and 2020-04 cohorts once they have 12 months of history.
  • Next step: refresh the cohort view monthly, and add a "no order in the previous 12 months" flag so new-customer cohorts can be defined cleanly once the history is long enough.
